# Copper February 2012 

- A strong start to the year quickly ran out of steam when it emerged that Chinese buyers failed to return to the market post Chinese New Year with quite the gusto that had been hoped.  Indeed, sluggish end use demand has resulted in firms taking a wait and see approach that was so evident in Europe in the final quarter of last year.  Moreover, with the arbitrage window closed and Chinese buyers reluctant to buy at prices near $8500/t, copper failed to build on the strong momentum from January and traded sideways through most of the month. 

- Changes over the course of the past month have resulted in only a modest tweak to our market balance this year, with the net result being that we now forecast a 100kt deficit.  The main adjustment in our forecast, however, is where we see the peak in prices.  The premature stock build from large scale Chinese cathode imports in Q4 2011 have taken away some of the anticipated price impact from the market this quarter.  We still remain of the opinion that Chinese demand improvements will be centred on the second half of the year and it is for this reason that we now project prices to peak in the third quarter at $8900, while we still expect full year prices to average $8700/t. 

- The nascent improvement in Europe and the US would be encouraging for global demand prospects were it not for the worryingly tepid conditions in China.  While much of the improvement in Europe could be ascribed to re-stocking by end users, this is far from the case in China where high stocks of finished goods and a lack of clarity in order books is hitting demand for cathode.  For the year as a whole we forecast global demand growth of 3.6%. 

- Thus far in this year’s Mating Season, with one notable exception, Japanese smelters have managed to hold the Freeport terms of $63.5/t & 6.35c/lb across the board.  The one exception apparently involved a deal between Sumitomo Metal Mining and Anglo Chile, with the two sides seemingly settling at $60.5/t & 6.05c/lb.  Taking into account the results of the Mating Season so far, it does seem that Japanese and European smelters have all but established a benchmark at $63.5/t & 6.35c/lb whereas in the rest of Asia and ignoring high-grade concentrate premia, there have been a wider spread of terms, ranging from $60/t & 6c/lb to $63.5/t & 6.35c/lb.

Copper Monthly Update 

## Market Developments 

**New year rally loses its appetite** A strong start to the year quickly ran out of steam when it emerged that Chinese buyers failed to return to the market post Chinese New Year with quite the gusto that had been hoped.  Indeed, sluggish end use demand has resulted in firms taking a wait and see approach that was so evident in Europe in the final quarter of last year.  Moreover, with the arbitrage window closed and Chinese buyers reluctant to buy at prices near $8500/t, copper failed to build on the strong momentum from January and traded sideways through most of the month. 

The rally at the start of the year was largely built on the premise that prices had been oversold at the end of 2011 and that fundamentals, in the shape of another forecast deficit, were reasserting themselves.  Indeed, Chinese firms were expected to come back from their holidays ready to place large orders and this would see prices well and truly break through the $8500 barrier and then who knows.  Or so the story went.  It turns out that after over-indulging at Chinese New Year, or perhaps on imports in the final quarter, China now feels a little bloated and lacks the appetite to buy in earnest, especially at current prices.  The absence of Chinese buyers and concern over whether this is indicative of a worse than expected outturn for demand this year has thus capped prices. 

**Near term tightness sees spreads dance into backwardation** The first week of February saw copper prices lack any real conviction amid ongoing concern over the European debt crisis and as traders pondered whether the start of year rally had gone too far too soon.  The high point for the year didn’t come until the second week of the month, when Greece agreed to tough new austerity measures that would pave the way for its second bail out.  This saw prices climb to $8737.5/t on 9<sup>th</sup> but this proved to be short-lived and cash quotes pulled back on increasing concerns about Chinese demand, which led to a six day losing streak with prices hitting their low for the month of $8169/t on 17<sup>th</sup> .  It was news that China would loosen credit somewhat by nudging banks’ reserve ratios lower by 50 basis points that snapped the losing run, although at the same time tightness in the cash to three month spread on the LME was also emerging.  This led to the market moving into backwardation on 23<sup>rd</sup> and further the following day, with open interest data pointing to short covering being behind the switch.  It is also worth noting that a modest upturn in European and North American copper demand, which had caused premia to continue to rise, and a general shortage of material as a result of ongoing LME stock declines, may also have contributed to the switch from contango.  Meanw

hile, we also understand that Glencore has needed to buy material to fulfil PASAR’s contractual commitments as we discussed in more detail last month. Further, with the arbitrage window closed, Chinese premia at low levels and with stocks already mounting both on and off exchange in China, it is possible that material which was on route to China may have been diverted to Asian LME warehouses to take advantage of the backwardation. Alternatively, material could move from increasing bonded warehouse stocks to be shipped to South Korea, just as happened a year ago. In addition to the switch to backwardation, copper prices also found support from dollar weakness and improved sentiment ahead of a cash injection from the European Central Bank. **Grasberg in new labour disruption** When we discussed the risks to supply last month we noted the likelihood of continued strike action and late in the month this has proved to be correct, although not necessarily from an expected source. Just as Freeport’s Grasberg operation was slowly ramping up, there is a new twist to labour problems there, this time as the company told workers to stay away as of the 23rd as it could not guarantee their safety amid reported intimidation and violence against those employees who did not take part in last year’s strike. It is worth noting that Grasberg is yet to lift the _force majeure_ that it declared during the strike. #### **Weekly copper exchange stocks and cash LME price** 1800 10000

Metals Market Service Monthly Update - February 2012 Page 2 of 21 Copper Monthly Update **LME stock slide masks overall rise in exchange stocks** Stocks on the LME have been on a downward overall trend since October of last year and hit a new low of 299kt on 27th of February. However, since the start of December SHFE exchange stocks have been on a sharp upward trajectory, adding over 150kt and hitting a decade high of 216kt at the end of February. There has been little movement in COMEX stocks but the net result is that overall exchange stocks, currently standing at around 600kt, are now at their highest level since September of last year. We note elsewhere in this report that the Chinese spot market is somewhat sluggish at present, with the result that spot sales of cathode are at a discount to the front month contract on SHFE. This is leading to material being sold on to the exchange in a bid to earn a better margin. Meanwhile, cancelled warrants seem to have peaked and are now beginning to wane after reaching c.95kt

at the start of February but have now edged lower to 89kt on 27th. Although this points to further withdrawals from LME warehouses, as we note, this does not necessarily imply lower exchange inventories overall, especially if material begins to accumulate in Asian LME locations. #### **Shanghai/LME arbitrage ($/t) vs refined copper imports** Refined Imports cash arbitrage 3-month arbitrage

**Chinese imports pull back from December high** Imports of copper into China fell in January, although this was far from surprising given the sharp run up in the final months of 2011; however, on a year-on-year basis shipments still grew by around a third. Indeed, imports of 335kt still represented one of the all time high figures, while this was also in a month where there was significant disruption from the Chinese New Year holidays. Material continued to flood in to China last month owing to the fact that the arbitrage window was open in late 2011. However, with the arbitrage window now firmly closed, Chinese demand sluggish and the LME in backwardation, any material en route to China right now may well be diverted to regional LME warehouses. Chinese demand has failed to pick up in earnest, or indeed at all, following the end of the Chinese New Year holidays, which has resulted in a dearth of activity in the Chinese spot market. Moreover, this is the time of year when we would also expect there to be an increase in commercial cathode stocks in China as firms start to spend a significant part of their annual budget on building inventories. However, the sluggish state of demand and lack of firm orders from end users have resulted in semis producers taking a cautious approach to buying metal. This is also being exacerbated by credit conditions remaining relatively tight despite the cut in the reserve ratio requirement, in addition to what are perceived as relatively high prices. Normally, the Chinese stocking phase would be accompanied by SHFE prices being above the LME, with the open arbitrage window drawing material into China. However, with a significant stock build already having taken place during the fourth quarter, even if this was more at the trader and speculator level, the big question for copper prices is whether the commercial restock will take place during the second quarter, or not at all. This will ultimately depend on copper prices, the arbitrage and the extent to which Chinese demand improves in the coming months. **Premia movements underscore demand differences** The movement of copper premia over the past month has underlined the relative health of regional demand, slumping in China but firming in Europe over t

he month. Chinese premia have plummeted to $20-50/t from around $100/t at the end of January amid lacklustre end use demand and mounting stock levels, although it was a different story in Europe where premia edged up from a month ago to around $60/t and while up by only $10/t on the prior month, this is double the levels of December, suggesting a nascent recovery in regional demand. As we discuss in our demand section, European semis producers are reporting a steady improvement in demand following the destock of the final quarter of last year, although this is mostly confined to northern Europe, and Germany in particular. In fact, some producers believe that the uplift in orders is more than just restocking but indicative of improving underlying demand, although it is perhaps too early to declare an end to regional economic travails. Meanwhile, the US is also experiencing a continuation of the mild upturn towards the end of last year, although premia have remained within a similar range to last month and as such, stand at 5.75c/lb. While much of the improvement in Europe could be ascribed to re-stocking by end users, this is far from the case in China where high stocks of finished goods and a lack of clarity in order books is hitting demand for cathode. For the year as a whole we forecast global demand growth of 3.6%. ### **Europe and CIS** **Major economies in reverse in 2012** When we wrote about the North-South divide in European economies in our previous publication we were trying to underline that to look at the overall growth in regional industrial activity is somewhat misleading. However, it is probably more accurate to call it the Germany and the rest divide rather than North to South as Germany is the only major industrial economy that still enjoyed some degree of growth in industrial production in December. However, Germany’s growth of 1.3% was the slowest pace in over two years. Meanwhile, there were contractions in output of varying degrees in Italy and Spain, while IP in France also slipped into negative territory. For the region as a whole, 2012 is undoubtedly going to be a tough year and we forecast a contraction in industrial output for each of the four major countries mentioned. **Aurubis calendar Q4 results underscore demand struggles** Hot on the heels of their calendar Q3 results, Aurubis has released its fourth quarter production figures, which revealed a plunge in output. In fact, wire rod production fell by 21.2% year on year to 156kt, while shapes output fell an even more severe 31.5% to 37kt. These figures are in line with our view of a major pull back in semis orders at the end of last year as end users chose to run down inventories amid economic uncertainty stemming from ongoing regional debt problems. #### **Aurubis Q4 wire rod production – (kt)** 120 240

Meanwhile, Aurubis has announced its intention to close its copper semis plant at Yverdon-Les-Bains in Switzerland as it seeks to streamline operations. Output of around 4kt per year of complex profiles will be transferred to Olen in Belgium, where production of profiles will be focussed. This rationalisation follows on from Aurubis announcing late last year that it is to close its semis plant at Finspang in Sweden. **Italian semis output down by 5% in 2011** In a similar vein to results from Aurubis noted above, Italian semis output fell away sharply in the fourth quarter of the year as demand ground to a halt. Indeed, copper semis production fell by 12.1% year on year in the fourth quarter, while copper alloy semis output declined by a similar 12.2%. This resulted in a full year contraction overall of 4.8% in semis including alloys in Italy in 2011 following the 18.6% expansion in 2010. **Rod mills off to a steady start** Since the start of the year, rod mills in particular have noted an upturn in order levels, although clearly, some parts of the region are doing better than others. In Germany for example, mills have seen customers placing orders again after withdrawing from business in the fourth quarter, with firms needing to modestly rebuild stocks. However, elsewhere, and in particular in southern Europe, things are less positive. It is too early to say whether the upturn is simply a reflection of re-stocking artificially and temporarily lifting consumption or whether end use demand is actually doing better than expected. However, we are taking a cautious view and still forecast a contraction in regional demand for this year as we highlight below. ### **Americas** **CDA issues downward revisions to US copper shipment data** With no new recent data available directly related to the copper sector, interested parties were left to ponder the heavy revisions to historic figures released this month by the Copper Development Association. Largely due apparently to double-counting, monthly shipment figures for copper wire rod as well as copper and alloy semis were each slashed by amounts averaging 4-6kt/quarter for 2011 and 2010, with the full-year

tally for 2009 also being pared back. For the first nine months of last year, wire rod shipments were down by 2% vs. the equivalent period of 2010 at 943kt, while copper and alloy semis shipments were off by 1.2% to 716kt. Again, due to data revisions, shipments of brass mill rod, bar and sections and copper tube rose by 7.8% and 5%, respectively, but deliveries of all other semis products declined. Looking at the final quarter of the year, we would expect a further contraction of rod shipments of around 5% on Q3, given the 7% cut in actual production in Q4 (at just 289.3kt) vs. Q3’s 311kt, leaving full year shipments of 1.234Mt, down by just 10kt vs. 2010’s 1.244Mt. #### **US brass mill shipments – (kt)** 20 100

Metals Market Service Monthly Update - February 2012 Page 6 of 21 Copper Monthly Update **Some (relative) strength noted in the housing sector** Our recent commentary that rod makers are optimistic for a 5% gain in production rates this year has been supported to some extent by recent macro economic data – even from the long-suffering housing and construction sector. Housing starts increased by 1.5% month on month to an annualised 699,000 units, propelled by a 14% gain in multi-unit buildings. Construction rates of apartment buildings are likely to be relatively strong this year, as the poor state of US household finances has increased demand for rental properties, pushing up rents. In year on year terms, total starts increased by 10%. US housing starts have fluctuated a great deal in the past few years around a very low level (from 1970 to 2007 housing starts never fell below 1 million per year) and there has been a number of false starts to any recovery. But there are signs that recovery could gain some momentum in 2012. The National Association of Home Builders said that its index of home-builder confidence rose for the fifth straight month in February. With the level of housing starts so low in 2011, if housing starts maintained January’s pace through 2012 we would see a gain for the year of 22%. As such, it would not be a surprise to see double digit growth this year. Meanwhile, US sales of existing homes rose to an 18-month high in January, reducing property supply to the lowest level seen in seven years. **Announced investments show confidence in US copper sectors** In spite of the long downtrend in US first-use copper demand, some companies remain sufficiently confident of the US and North America’s ultimate metal offtake to continue investing in new facilities. This month Xinxiang City, Henan-based Golden Dragon Precise Copper Tube Inc., which claims to

be the largest manufacturer of ACR copper tube in Asia, increased the size of its planned new investment in Alabama that it announced initially about eight months ago.  It will now build a US$100M plant at Pine Hill, Wilcox County in Alabama, using cast and roll tube-making technology, and this should allow the company to avoid getting hit by anti-competitive trade legislation which has affected its imports into the US from plants in China and Mexico.  Plant capacity and start-up time have yet to be released, though we would expect no less than 8kt/a due to the economics of such a unit, and probably much larger at between 30-50kt/a, given the company’s existing presence in the sector.  Cast and roll tube technology came about in the early 1990s from Outokumpu/UpCast, and was subsequently taken up by Italy’s Danieli via its own “Endless Copper Tube” (ECT) technology and by Germany’s Mannesmann when interest from UpCast fell away in the mid-2000s.  Chinese manufacturers have since made versions of their own, and we assume at this point that Golden Dragon indeed uses its own variant.  At the copper rod level, the SDI-La Farga copper rod plant investment in Indiana will come on stream during Q2 this year, but using 100% scrap rather than new metal. And, further downstream, cable industry giant Nexans added to its North American presence mid-month by buying El Dorado, AR-based AmerCable, which produces cable for harsh environments such as on- and off-shore oil and gas and the renewable energy sectors.  The transaction cost was US$275M.  Last year, Nexans announced an US$80M investment in a new extra high voltage underground cable plant, which is expected to start up mid-2013. 

### **China** 

**Slow start to Chinese demand** The start of the year has brought with it little clarity on the demand outlook in China. Looking back to a year ago, it seems that there is a good deal of similarity between now and then, with firm growth expected and the first signals of this ought to be firming premia and rising imports.  Last year, the draw in stocks that took place through the first half masked these signals and with the strong shipments into the country at the end of 2011 and in the first month of this year also, it looks likely that consumption will be met from inventories for the time being. However, discussions with market participants indicate that demand is relatively sluggish at present, with the seasonal upturn yet to happen.  The timing and extent of this upturn will have wide reaching consequences not just for Chinese and global consumption growth this year, but also for copper price movements. 

**Credit remains tight, despite RRR cut** The major economic news out of China over the past month has been the cut in the reserve ratio requirement, which should allow banks to lend more.  The Peoples Bank of China announced a money supply growth target for 2012 of 14%, the same as 2011 and a relatively conservative target.  In short, monetary policy is ea

sing slightly but the authorities are being cautious not to ease too much too soon. China has plenty of scope to carry out stimulus if it chooses, so expect to see further developments should the economic outlook deteriorate. In fact, even without further stimulus, China’s government is looking to support fixed asset investment growth by promoting the start of new infrastructure projects, the State Council said. Details at this point are lacking, but comments from the NDRC research centre suggest that state-led infrastructure investment may grow by 15-20% in 2012 - a large increase over 2011 and similar to that of 2010. **Semis output lacks bite** Any hopes for a swift upturn in semis output and demand following the Chinese New Year holidays have been dashed as activity at mills remains subdued at best. Despite inventories of some end use goods having been worked down a little, semis producers report sluggish order books. Indeed, wire rod producers are running at around 70% of that which they would expect to be producing typically. **Lack of new projects tempering electrical sector** Part of the reason for lacklustre wire rod output is weak production of power cable amid an absence of new energy projects at the moment. As we noted above, however, China is expected to invest heavily in infrastructure this year, with growth of 15-20% anticipated, although this is yet to feed through into real demand. We also expect reasonable growth for construction, even if not at the same pace of recent years, despite reports of widespread doom and gloom in the sector as social housing starts made at the end of 2011 support demand for copper this year. Meanwhile, recent announcements aimed to help first time buyers should also help the sector, if only in mopping up some of the unsold properties, which is needed before the sector can recover in earnest. In December, production fell by 9% year on year, but this was largely due to December 2010 being a very strong month due to the expiration of incentive schemes. In fact, monthly production volumes increased in November and December on a month-on-month basis, reversing some of the losses recorded earlier in the year. This ties in with our expectations of a gradual improvement in China auto sales and production through 2012, which will be supportive of copper demand also. **8% growth projection reiterated** We noted above that there is a lack of clarity in the market on the current state of demand, however, this does not alter our conviction of a relatively robust year for overall demand. Certainly, much of the growth will become visible in the second half of the year, if only because of base effects. Even in a situation where imports remain sluggish through the first half, this will likely sow the seeds for stronger imports in the second half of the year and in any case, we are more concerned with measuring real demand than _apparent_ consumption. Metals Market Service Monthly Update - February 2012 Page 8 of 21 Copper Monthly Update ### **Japan** **2011 demand estimate nudged lower** Japan’s economic growth prospects deteriorated through Q4 2011 as supply chains were disrupted by floods in Thailand and the strong yen continued to reduce export competitiveness. Preliminary figures showed that real GDP fell 0.6% between October and December. For 2011 overall, GDP is estimated to have fallen by 0.9%. This deterioration in economic activity has led us to reduce our assessment of refined copper demand for 2011 and we now estimate that refined copper consumption declined by 4.3% in 2011 to 1.014Mt. **Economic drivers will underpin consumption growth** We expect modest economic growth to resume from the first quarter of 2012, although Q1 is likely to be challenging for exports in particular. Given the poor global outlook and the potential for contraction during H1, we have trimmed our 2012

IP forecast slightly.  However, there are some underlying drivers of growth.  Public investment spending is rising sharply, reflecting the government’s efforts in post-quake reconstruction, and this is likely to gain momentum through the year and support demand for copper semis in tandem. 

**PMI indicators suggest an improving outlook** Both the output and new orders indices rose above 50 in January, while the stocks of purchases continued to contract.  A combination of higher orders and lower inventories imply higher production in the future.  All these macro economic indicators should feed into stronger demand for copper which is now expected to expand by around 2.5% this year.  Shipments of copper semis should begin to show some recovery from Q2 onwards, supported by the anticipated recovery for appliances and the ongoing recovery in the automotive sectors.  Our latest data suggest a 13% rise in automotive production (13.8% increase in car production and 9.6% increase in commercial vehicle production) which will boost shipments of wiring harnesses and winding wire as well as sheet and strip for connectors. 

**Re-stock to boost brass mill sector** The brass mills sector experienced a de-stocking phase in 2011, with output falling 4.9% year-on-year.  Output was dented by weak shipments to both the chip and electronics parts makers reflecting a build up in inventories of end-products such as flat screen TVs and PCs.  These weak end-use markets also led to a sharp decline in output of copper and brass strip, declining 9.3% and 7.7% respectively year-on-year.  We do expect to see some recovery from the brass mills sector as the market enters a re-stocking phase. 

**Electrical sector to power down** By April 2012 all nuclear power generating capacity will be closed, and currently it does not seem likely that any reactors will restart before Q4 2012. As a result, demand from utilities is expected to be the worst performing segment.  Utilities have had to reassign their spending to focus on imports of coal and oil.  This has been at a cost to the development, construction and repair and maintenance of power transmission and distribution grid facilities.  These delays to the planned expenditure on power cables to support the network could also increase the risk of power constraints this year, particularly during the summer months. 

**Construction data suggests sector will build on 2011** In contrast to weakness in the power sector, shipments of wire and cable products to the construction sector rose 7.2% in 2011, while those from Japanese brass mills registered double digit growth of 12.4%.  This is supported by data for construction investment from the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism, which show monthly year-on-year increases since June 2011.  Housing starts are also showing improvement, suggesting a further pick up in copper consumption as the year progresses given that copper is consumed at the end rather than the beginn

ing of the construction cycle. The recovery in the construction sector will also drive additional demand for copper tube from the air conditioning and refrigeration sector which saw shipments up just shy of 6% in 2011. **A risky business** There are some (significant) risks to the short term outlook, namely the appreciation of the yen against the dollar and the euro, which has resulted in a sharp drop in competitiveness for Japanese manufacturers. Some major electronics corporations such as Sony are currently operating at a loss and are questioning whether it makes sense to continue to manufacture in Japan, while competition from Korean and Taiwanese manufacturers has also escalated. This could dent shipments of semi conductors and connectors in the short term, after recording 11% and 8% declines respectively in 2011. **Yen strength a concern** The global conditions that helped cause the appreciation of the yen and dent exports (European crisis, high uncertainty, negative real interest rates on government debt in countries such as US, Germany and UK) look set to remain in the short term, and as such a depreciation of the yen is unlikely in 2012. There is a real risk of closures of manufacturing capacity in Japan as a result of the strong yen as manufacturers look to further accelerate the establishment and expansion of offshore facilities into lower cost locations such as China, ASEAN, the Indian Subcontinent, Eastern Europe and North Africa. ## Concentrate Markets 

**Shipping delays and Grasberg issues maintain market tightness** Last month we noted that the concentrates market had directed its attention towards the custom smelting sector following the temporary closure of two major Asian plants. Since then the larger of the two, Saganoseki (400kt/a), has re-opened, with any loss in production expected to be mitigated by a shorter maintenance shutdown at sister-operation, Tamano.  Meanwhile, the 180kt/a Pasar smelter in the Philippines remained closed with the company issuing notices to customers of a likely re-start towards the end of the first half of this year.  Given the prolonged nature of this shutdown, one might be forgiven for expecting an easing in general concentrate availability.  However, the prevailing market situation remains far from ‘easy’ with Sterlite’s Tuticorin smelter having shut down for a week in the middle of February in part due to a backlog of vessels, linked to a legal dispute involving the freezing of maritime assets belonging to a Greek bulker operator.  At the same time, Hindalco’s Dahej smelter has thus far avoided a closure although inventories at the plant are also well below normal levels.  While part of the problem has been on account of these shipping delays, ongoing issues at Grasberg have also contributed to the Indian smelters’ woes.  The production ramp up at this Indonesian mining complex has been well below expectations, with concentrate output achieving only 50 to 60% of target since the start of the year.  Moreover, labour issues between previously striking and non-striking members have flared up of late to a point where production was suspended again on February 23<sup>rd</sup> for safety and security reasons.  With the exception of its Spanish smelting subsidiary, all of Grasberg’s concentrate sales are to customers in Asia.  Foll

owing the surge of spot business from the trade in China during January in response to the smelter closures mentioned above, the urgency to sell has now subsided, leading to a reduction in spot rates, from an average of $45/t & 4.5c/lb last month, to around $41/t & 4.1c/lb now. That said we understand that there was a further deterioration in terms towards month end into the mid 30s & 3s. ## Blister/anode and scrap markets 

**China scrap imports down by 37.2% in Jan 2012** According to customs statistics, China’s copper scrap imports were just 229kt in January, down by 37.2% on the same month last year.  This ties in with reports that of many of the country’s larger secondary smelters and refiners are struggling to secure sufficient scrap supplies and that some plants have been operating at only 50% of capacity,  This situation has been exacerbated by a deteriorating arbitrage between SHFE and Comex prices and rising costs at many of China’s disassembly yards.  In the US, No.2 scrap spreads for the export markets

widened through to the middle of the month to around 45c/lb below May Comex and then narrowed over the second half of February to 40c/lb in tandem with weaker copper prices. 

**Another Southern Copper blister tender issued in February** Southern Copper was once again active in the blister market with a further 1.5kt on sale for March shipment.  The company’s previous tender last month attracted a winning bid of approximately $70/t. 

**Chinese blister terms unchanged over last month** Chinese indicative spot blister RCs remained unchanged this month, with the deteriorating price arbitrage offset by a general lack of scrap.  Meanwhile in Europe, scrap supplies are somewhat easier in comparison with January and indicative blister terms have increased to around $100/t.

## Production news 

**Chilean refined metal production slips by 4.7% in 2010…** According to data from Cochilco in Chile, national refined metal output slipped by 4.7% last year on 2010 to 3.09Mt.  SxEw-sourced cathode output fell by 3.1% to 2.02Mt, while electro-refined cathode production fell by 5.3% to a shade under 1Mt.  At the mining level, national output fell by 3.2% to 5.244Mt.  The most notable declines came at Escondida (down by 24.7% to 817kt Cu contained in product), Collahuasi (down by 10% to 453kt) and Quebrada Blanca (down 26.7% to 63.4kt). 

**Codelco’s mine output recovers…** Of that 5.244Mt nationwide tally, Codelco’s operations accounted for c.1.796Mt, _vs._ 1.76Mt in 2010 (including its 49% stake in El Abra).  The 2% improvement here largely came from a 24% hike at Andina (188.5kt in 2010 _vs._ 234.4kt in 2011), following expansion work which should bring the mine back up towards 250-260kt this year.  Meanwhile, the 10kt increase in output at the Chuquicamata/Radomiro Tomic complex also helped to offset small year-on-year losses at Salvador and El Teniente, but Gaby remained a disappointment.  Having worked through some technical issues associated with its expansion programme and secured a new labour agreement last year, early 2011 expectations were that SxEw output there would rise to 160kt last year.  However, metal output of 118kt was little changed on 2010, although production recovered to an annualised rate of c.140kt/a in the fourth quarter. 

**..but Collahuasi and Mantos Blancos hold back Anglo Chile** Anticipated lower grades, coupled with abnormally high rainfall and heavy snow (which has continued into t

his first quarter, albeit with no announced work stoppage), repairs to a conveyor belt in September plus a strike in November, restrained copper output at the Collahuasi complex, where the major owners are Anglo American Chile and Xstrata (44% each).  Production fell by 10% or so, to 453.3kt from 2010’s 504kt.  Lower grades drove output down at Mantos Blancos (73kt in 2011 vs. 79kt a year prior) and at Mantoverde (58.5kt vs. 61kt).  However, these losses were partially offset by the Q4 expansion at Los Bronces (221.8kt vs 217kt) and higher ore grades at El Soldado (46.9kt vs. 40kt in 2010).  Following the expansion, mill output from Los Bronces should increase to in excess of 420kt copper in concentrate this year from 180kt last year, with SxEw production rates remaining unchanged at between 40-50kt/a.

**BHPB authorises capex at Escondida…** As expected, output from BHPB’s 57%-held Escondida mine fell considerably last year, by almost 25% to 818kt contained copper in concentrate (536kt) and cathode (283kt).  Planned low grade ore was largely accountable, although a near two-week labour-related stoppage also contributed to the fall.  The decline will be arrested in coming years, though, as BHPB and partners Rio Tinto and Japanese associates recently approved a total US$3.8B investment plan which will return the complex to former glories of 1.3-1.4Bt/a copper last seen during 2006 and 2007.  The current Los Colorados concentrator will be removed to allow access to higher grade ores, and a new, larger mill will be erected in its stead.  Secondly, a new oxide leaching area will be built to replace the existing facilities which will see cathode output rise from the 300-330kt of recent years to 385kt/a from 2014/2015.  A dramatic increase in reserves and total resources at the mine, following extensive fill-in exploration programmes, has underpinned these investments.

**..presses Pinto Valley back into action…** In its annual results presentation, BHPB also noted that it would bring the mill at its Pinto Valley property 125km east of Phoenix

in Arizona, USA back on line.  The mill last operated from late2007 until early 2009, and produced 53kt copper in concentrate during 2008.  The company says the mill will re-start at around that level by the end of this year, slightly lower than the average 71kt/a during the six-year period 1992-1997. Pinto Valley has maintained a low level of cathode output from SxEw operations since the early 1990s at a rate of c.6kt/a. 

**..while Teck gets a new labour contract at Quebrada Blanca** A week past the expiration date of its former labour contract agreement at Quebrada Blanca in Chile, Teck was able to announce a new settlement that should see the operation through to November 2015.  Last month we were concerned that the January 31<sup>st</sup> deadline would pass with no announcement of progress being made, placing 80kt/a copper at risk of a halt in production.  The period covering the new agreement will likely see a decision being made on an expansion to production from sulphide resources, with initial output of 90-100kt contained copper coming in 2017 and doubling within two years; Teck will submit an environment impact assessment report to Chilean authorities during Q2 this year.  For now, Quebrada Blanca is in a period of transition from a high grade heap leach operation to a low grade dump leach facility, and this became evident with the decline in output last year to 63.4kt from 86kt in 2010.  Teck expects this year’s production to be between 65-70kt. 

**Grupo Mexico hits Buenavista targets in 2011, outlines increases this year…** Preliminary data for Grupo Mexico show a successful ramp-up at its Buenavista (Cananea) copper division in Sonora, northern Mexico last year, following the lengthy strike which ended during 2010.  Our estimate of 170kt copper from combined sulphide and SxEw operations was only marginally off the actual 172.5kt, and the company advised this month that output for this year will edge up a notch, to 180kt.  Furthermore, Buenavista will benefit from new SxEw equipment for its expansion from 88kt/a capacity to a planned 120kt/a; the equipment was headed for the company’s Tia Maria project in Peru, but has been re-directed to Buenavista following the scheduling changes taking place at Tia Maria.  This will contribute to the increase in total annual capacity at Buenavista from the current 180kt/a to 488kt/a by 2015, 18 months earlier than planned.  As part of this year’s US$1.746B approved capital for expansion this year, Buenavista will receive US$322M for its concentrator section and a further US$164M for other equipment and US$155M for the SxEw III expansion. 

**..and approves capex in the USA and Peru** Elsewhere, Grupo Mexico continues to advance capex funds for its fiveyear expansion programme which should increase overall copper output from 0.8Mt/a to 1.4Mt/a.  Cuajone, in Peru, will receive US$154M for the expansion of its mine and mill this year, which should see output increase by 50-60kt/a from today’s 150-16

0kt/a.  Toquepala will also get US$201M on the way to doubling its production to c.300kt/a by 2018.  And the Mission complex in Arizona will have US$84M allocated this year for its expansion from the current 65-70kt/a to 7580kt/a by Q2 2013.  Studies are also underway at Mission to re-open the molybdenum plant.  If successful, the 2.6kt/a Mo unit would re-start by early 2013.  Meanwhile, the transfer of SxEw equipment from Tia Maria to Buenavista reflects the need to initiate a new environmental impact study at the Peruvian site which will incorporate the recent guidelines set by the new government.  The company now expects the 120kt/a project to start up in 2015, but with this delay and the local opposition which remains, we anticipate 2022 will be more likely. 

**Pyshma boosts anode capacity** Russia’s largest copper refinery in the Urals, Uralelectromed’s (UE) Pyshma, can be expected to have more anodes available from this March now that it has commissioned the new anode casting wheels supplied in 2007 by SMS Meer.  Pyshma has no dedicated smelter, and receives blister from the four regional smelters of Kirovgrad (a Uralelectromed subsidiary since 2001), Krasnouralsk (UE’s Svyatogor subsidiary), Mednogorsk and Sredneuralsk.  We had originally understood that this latest investment in anode casting equipment would allow Pyshma to maintain an adequate supply of anodes for its electrolytic refinery which was rated at 380kt/a capacity up until the end of last year.  This would allow some of the less efficient areas of the anode preparation and refinery areas (which date from the mid-1930s) to be phased out.  However, Pyshma has stated that its 1.2B rouble investment plan, which was approved in 2004-2005 and began in 2006, will increase anode capacity to 570kt/a.  Furthermore, the four in-house old anode furnaces + new casting wheels combination is capable of producing two sizes of anode simultaneously: one for the new refinery tankhouse and one for the old.  This slightly exceeds planned _new_ cathode capacity of 0.53Mt/a.  The new refinery tankhouse, for which the final four (out of 448) cells were delivered from CTI in Ghent, Belgium last December, has a rated capacity of 150kt/a and came with a capex tag of US$130M.  We believe Pyshma’s cathode output has been close to capacity for the last five years or so, and with the company having achieved “good delivery” status from the LME in mid-2010, much of the cathode leaving Pyshma can target a wider market outside Russia. However, with the tax on Russian cathode exports in place since December 2010, it is likely that Pyshma has made greater use of its in-house Katur-Invest wire rod facility (a subsidiary company), which has had c.300kt/a Contirod capacity since 1999 and is located on the Pyshma site. 

**Mitsubishi Corp takes position in Quellaveco** Mitsubishi Corp has boosted its copper investments by taking up the 18.1% stake in the Quellaveco project that has been held by the International Fin

ance Corp for an unstated sum. Located in southern Peru at Moquegua, the Quellaveco project is 81.9%-owned by Anglo American and is currently at the feasibility stage. Anglo is in the process of obtaining permits required to take the project through to Board approval. Anticipated capex of US$3B should see output of 215kt/a copper in concentrate (plus Mo and Ag by-products) from 2018 following a 2017 start, levelling off to 160kt/a by year four. Metals Market Service Monthly Update - February 2012 Page 14 of 21 Copper Monthly Update **Nevada Copper moves Pumpkin Hollow along with FS** Nevada Copper Corp completed its feasibility study on the Pumpkin Hollow project at Yerington in western Nevada last month, and has already begun shaft-sinking work. The FS calls for a combined 55kt/d open pit and 5kt/d underground mine feeding a single 60kt/d mill. Proposed output should average 124kt/a over the first five years, with c.100kt/a suggested over the 18 year life-of-mine operating rate. Initial capital of c.US$1B is anticipated, with cash production costs of US$1.28/lb Cu inclusive of gold and silver by-product revenue streams. An update to the FS should be completed by mid-year, and if permits can be in hand by early 2013 a production start of Q2 2015 is currently being targeted by the company.
